Then, tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

When the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of the group went to Lake Manasa, one-eighth of them flew from the edge of the water to the grove of land-lotuses, and three pairs of swans were seen playing with great affection in the water, which was beautiful with soft lotus stalks. Then, say, how many swans were in that group? (3)

Vasudeva is the supreme Brahman. His manifestation is the supreme Person <note>original: "Purusha"</note>; He is unmanifest, devoid of qualities <note>original: "nirguna"</note>, tranquil, beyond the twenty-five principles <note>original: "tattvas"</note>, and immutable, meaning He is without change. 12.

->The god, abiding within nature, pervades everything both inside and out.<-
->Sankarshana, at the beginning of creation, created the waters and deposited his seed within them. 13.<-

The author explains that since it is impossible for the pure Brahman to be the cause of the world, he says: "Abiding within nature," meaning qualified by <term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>, and "pervading everything inside and out," because He is the material cause of the world. All these attributes are to be understood as belonging to Sankarshana, who is a portion of Vasudeva, by realizing his identity with Vasudeva. Sankarshana, who is a portion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he deposited his "seed," a specific power. 13.

The god Sankarshana, who is everywhere perceptible, entered into this very nature and first created the waters. Afterward, he placed his own energy in the form of a seed into that water. 13.

->That egg became golden and was covered in darkness on all sides.<-
->There, Aniruddha, the eternal one, became manifest first. 14.<-

The author now explains what happened next. That water, combined with his energy, became a golden, spherical egg, covered everywhere by darkness both inside and out. The meaning is that a golden egg was born in the space filled with darkness. In that golden egg, Aniruddha, the eternal one—who is Sankarshana, a portion of Vasudeva, because he is in the form of a portion—became manifest first. He was not born, as the doctrine of pre-existing effects is accepted. Just as oil exists in sesame seeds and is merely manifested, not created. 14.

That energy in the form of a seed took the shape of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There (inside the egg), the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. 14.

->This Lord is recited in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha.<-
->He is indeed called Aditya because he was the first being, and because of his expansion, he is called Surya. 15.<-

Now, for the better understanding of the people, the author provides his other names. This Lord Aniruddha, who is a portion of Sankarshana and endowed with the six qualities of divine majesty <note>original: "shaidgunya-aishvarya"</note>, is recited or described in the Vedas as Hiranyagarbha because he dwells inside the golden egg. The meaning is that his other well-known name in the Vedas is Hiranyagarbha. He is indeed called Aditya because he was the first to be manifested. Because he expanded to create this world, he is called Surya.

"Hiranyagarbha existed in the beginning; he was the sole lord of all created beings."

This is the scriptural testimony. 15.

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who today offers this speech to you two,**
**Bestow upon him great heroic power, prosperity of cattle, and good horses. <note>Verse 2</note>**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma | He who | today | to you two | this | speech | honors.**
**To him | bestow | good-heroic-power | of cows | prosperity | good-horsed.**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, the **sacrificer who today, in this ritual, offers this speech** (in the form of a hymn) **to you two**—that is, for your sake—honors you. **Bestow upon that sacrificer prosperity** (growth) **of cows** (cattle). What kind of prosperity? One possessing **good heroic power**, accompanied by excellent strength, and **possessing good horses**. Regarding the word *gavam* (of cows), the accent on the case-ending—which would normally occur due to the rule 'savekach'—is prevented by the rule 'na goshvan savavarnai' (accent is not shifted in certain forms of 'go' and 'ashva').

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, he who would give an offering to you, he who would give a sacrifice prepared with oblations,**
**He, with progeny and heroic power, shall attain a full life. <note>Verse 3</note>**

->Pada-patha<-
**Agni-Soma | He who | offering | he who | to you two | would give | oblation-preparation.**
**He | with progeny | good-heroic-power | all | life | attains.**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, **the sacrificer who offers an oblation** (such as clarified butter) **to you two**, or **who offers an oblation prepared with** ritual materials like *charu* (sacrificial porridge) and *purudasha* (sacrificial cake), **that sacrificer**, endowed **with progeny** (sons and grandsons) and **good heroic power**, shall **attain a full life** (the entire span of existence). Regarding the word *ahutim* (offering): by the rule 'juhoteh ktini tadau cha', the radical accent is retained. Regarding *dashat* (would give): from the root *dash* (to give); it takes the 'let' (Vedic subjunctive) augment 'at'. Because it is connected to a relative pronoun, it is subject to the 'anighata' (lack of accent) rule. Regarding *havishkritim* (oblation-preparation): the offering in which the preparation of the oblation occurs. In a *bahuvrihi* compound, the first member retains its original accent.

# But from meditating on the Supreme, that which is obscured; from that, the bondage and liberation of this one occur. 3.2.5.

It might be argued: The individual soul (<term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual consciousness</gloss>) is merely a part of the Supreme Self, like a spark from a fire. If this is so, just as the spark shares the same power of burning and illuminating as the fire, the individual soul and the Lord (<term>ishvara</term> <gloss>the Supreme Ruler</gloss>) must share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, through the power of its knowledge and sovereignty, the individual soul would be able to create chariots and other objects in a dream through mere will. 

To this, we reply: While the relationship between the individual soul and the Lord is that of part and whole, the individual soul's possession of qualities opposite to those of the Lord is a matter of direct experience. Does this mean the individual soul lacks the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it does not lack them. Though they exist, they are obscured by the veil of ignorance (<term>avidya</term> <gloss>primordial ignorance</gloss>) and similar factors. 

This obscured power manifests only in a being who strives, who meditates on the Supreme Lord, and whose darkness has been dispelled—just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, becomes clear through the strength of medicine. It manifests through the grace of the Lord, not by nature for all beings. Why? Because it is from that cause, the Lord, that the bondage and liberation of this soul occur; bondage arises from not knowing the nature of the Lord, and liberation arises from knowing that nature. Thus, the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, the third state <note>referring to the state beyond waking and dreaming</note> is attained at the dissolution of the body, where one becomes the master of all and reaches all desires."

# Or it is so because of connection with a body. 3.2.6.

Why is the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured? It is logical that these powers should remain unobscured, as the power of a spark to burn and illuminate remains. We respond: This is true. However, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of its connection with a body—the connection with the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. 

There is an analogy here: just as the burning and illuminating powers of fire, even though present, become obscured when the fire is contained within a piece of wood, or covered by ashes, so too does the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occur due to its connection with the body, which is composed of names and forms created by ignorance, and the resulting confusion of identity. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to address the doubt regarding the soul being distinct from the Lord. 

If one suggests that the soul is indeed distinct from the Lord because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured, and that we need not postulate a connection to a body, we say: No. The distinctness of the soul from the Lord is not tenable. The text begins with "That Deity perceived" and continues, "I shall enter these beings with this individual soul" <note>original: "Anena jivenatmana anupravishya"</note>, referring to the soul as the Self. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its divinity: "That is the Truth, that is the Self, you are That, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but it becomes one whose knowledge and sovereignty are obscured due to its connection with a body. 

Because of this, the creation of chariots and other objects in a dream by the soul's will is not possible. If the creation in a dream were merely by will, no one would see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is undesirable. As for the argument that the experience of the waking world proves the reality of the dream world, that comparison is not intended to suggest reality, as it would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of chariots and such in a dream. That comparison simply means the dream is similar to the waking state because it is caused by impressions (<term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious tendencies</gloss>) resulting from waking experiences. Therefore, the conclusion that the dream is mere illusion (<term>maya-matra</term> <gloss>only an appearance</gloss>) is well-founded.

# Its absence is in the channels, the heart-membrane, and the Self, according to scripture. 3.2.7.

The Section on its Absence.

The state of dreaming has been examined. Now, the state of deep sleep (<term>sushupti</term> <gloss>dreamless sleep</gloss>) is examined. There are various scriptural passages regarding deep sleep. In one place, it is heard: "When this person is asleep, having become completely serene, and knows no dream, he has entered these channels (<term>nadi</term> <gloss>subtle energy channels</gloss>)." In another place, having mentioned the channels, it is heard: "Having moved through them, he rests in the heart-membrane (<term>puritat</term> <gloss>the pericardium</gloss>)." Elsewhere, after mentioning the channels: "He abides in them when he is asleep and sees no dreams; then in this very vital force (<term>prana</term> <gloss>life breath</gloss>) he becomes one." Elsewhere: "He rests in that space which is within the heart." Elsewhere: "O gentle one, then he becomes united with the Pure Being, he attains his own nature." And also: "Embraced by the intelligent Self, he knows nothing external or internal." 

Here is the doubt: Are these—the channels and the rest—separate places for deep sleep, independent of one another, or is there one place for deep sleep, with them being mutually dependent? What is the initial position? They are separate, because they serve the same purpose, and things serving the same purpose are never found to be mutually dependent anywhere...

## From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable motion for the body. The state of having disembodied senses is the attainment of the function of the disembodied senses in accordance with the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like or sweet-symbolized</gloss>. These are attained through the conquest of the five forms of the senses ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience ॥ 49 ॥

For one who remains in the state where the pure conscious principle is distinguished from the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>the luminous or purity-aspect of mind</gloss>—which has been cleansed of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> <gloss>activity/passion</gloss> and <term>tamas</term> <gloss>inertia/darkness</gloss>—having attained the supreme clarity and the final stage of detachment, there is sovereignty over all states of being. The author speaks of the accomplishments arising from the conquest of the five forms of the senses: **From that comes speed of mind, the state of having disembodied senses, and mastery over the primal matter.** The state of the senses being disembodied refers to their capacity to function without the physical body. Place refers to regions like Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and other periods. Object refers to subtle objects and so forth. Conquest of the primal matter is the state of having control over all modifications of nature through the conquest of the senses connected with them. These accomplishments are termed <term>madhupratīkā</term> by those expert in the science of yoga. One might ask: if the senses are conquered and become subservient along with their objects, what does this have to do with the primal matter and its causes? To this, he replies: **These are attained through the conquest of the five forms.** This refers to the five forms of the senses, such as grasping and others. The meaning is this: these accomplishments do not arise from the conquest of the senses alone, but from the conquest of the five forms, which include the primal matter and its derivatives within them ॥ 48 ॥

These are the <term>samyamas</term> <gloss>concentrated practices</gloss> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. By directly or indirectly establishing faith, they lead to the intermediate manifestations of that discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, which is the ultimate goal. He explains: **For one established solely in the discriminative discernment between the pure conscious principle and the sattva-aspect of mind, there is sovereignty over all states of existence and omniscience.** Clarity arises from the removal of the impurities of <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term>. Following this comes the supreme state of detachment. The mind-stuff was previously overwhelmed by <term>rajas</term> and <term>tamas</term> and was not under control. When these are stilled, the yogi who has attained mastery establishes the mind solely in the discernment between the pure conscious principle and the <term>sattva</term>-aspect of mind, leading to sovereignty over all states of existence. <margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing but striving for learning, hearing and seeing more each day, yet having no way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said, "Hear much, choose what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one comes to know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss>, looking back, all acts of pretense are false. To remove falsehood and restore one's nature is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten and becomes pure, and the nature is restored, this is called diminishing. If the false is not yet fully removed, even to the point of forgetting the act of forgetting, the mind cannot be pure and restore the nature without remainder. Only then can one act without losing the state of non-action. People all have the desire to seize the world and the reasoning behind things, so they initiate affairs and seek to control them. When the heart is revealed externally, things will dislike it, which makes success impossible. The sage performs non-action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is revealed externally, things find peace. Although he does not seek to control the world or its reasoning, because he acts this way, the world and its reasoning become harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> Engaging in learning means one has not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Not having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must be broad in seeking it, therefore it is said, "increase." Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> means one has already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must inevitably practice non-action, therefore it is said, "diminish." Diminishing and further diminishing still does not escape from having intentional action. One must also diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action means there is no intentional action, which is called being silent and unmoved. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" refers to the state where, upon being stimulated, one perfectly comprehends all the affairs of the world. To act through non-action to reach the ultimate non-action is what is meant by the constant. Learning that is free from worry is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the <term>Tao</term>. Who but the most divine can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action; if one uses intentional action, it is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, so learning aims to increase day by day. Only after one can do anything can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>, so the <term>Tao</term> aims to diminish day by day. Yet, "increasing" is something one can pursue, while "diminishing" is perhaps difficult to force. Only those with the utmost clarity can instantly cast off their burdens and arrive at the state of non-action. Thus, they can act in such a way that nothing is left undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Engaging in learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, thus it increases day by day. Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> is for the sake of removing falsehood, thus it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach the limit, the diminishing will be incomplete; thus, the "increasing" is the foundation for the "diminishing." If one diminishes and diminishes again until falsehood is gone and the truth is complete, then one arrives at non-action. When one reaches non-action, there is nothing one does that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When it comes to the height of non-action, even though the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs through intentional action, it is hard to find a moment of peace. If even one thing creates entanglement and contradiction, how much more so with the complexity of the whole world?

The sage has no constant mind. He makes the hearts of the common people his own heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for the <term>De</term> <gloss>Virtue/Power</gloss> of goodness is attained. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for the <term>De</term> of trust is attained. Just as, venerable sir, a dust-cloth wipes clean things and wipes dirty things, wipes away excrement and wipes away urine, wipes away saliva, wipes away pus, and wipes away blood, and the dust-cloth is neither troubled nor disgusted by it; just so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth, expansive, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, free from ill-will. Whoever, venerable sir, does not have mindfulness directed toward the body established in their own body, such a person might offend a fellow practitioner and depart on their journey without having representation made amends.

Just as, venerable sir, an outcaste boy or an outcaste girl, with a basket in hand, wearing ragged clothes <note>original: "nantikavāsī"</note>, enters a village or a town with a lowly mind; just so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste boy, expansive, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, free from ill-will. Whoever, venerable sir, does not have mindfulness directed toward the body established in their own body, such a person might offend a fellow practitioner and depart on their journey without having made amends.

13. Chapter on Happy Conduct

<margin>K 275</margin>
N 180

Then, the young prince Mañjuśrī spoke to the Blessed One: "It is difficult, Blessed One, extremely difficult, what these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas have endured out of respect for the Blessed One. How, Blessed One, should these bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period?"

When this was said, the Blessed One replied to the young prince Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in four dharmas. In which four?

Here, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva should preach this discourse on the Dharma in the final age, in the final period, having established himself in proper conduct and proper spheres of association <note>original: "ācāragocara" — conduct and range/sphere of activity</note>. And how, Mañjuśrī, is a bodhisattva and mahāsattva established in proper conduct?

When, Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva and mahāsattva is patient, disciplined, having attained the stage of discipline, with a mind that is fearless and unagitated, and free from jealousy; when the bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not practice <note>or "dwell upon"</note> any dharma, and observes the true nature of all phenomena <note>original: "svalakṣaṇa" — own-mark/individual characteristic</note>. That which is without grasping and without conceptualization in these dharmas, this is called the conduct of the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī.

<margin>K 276</margin>
W 236
And what is the sphere of association for the bodhisattva and mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī? When the bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not associate with kings, nor with princes, nor with high-ranking ministers, nor with government officials; he does not serve them, frequent them, wait upon them, or visit them. He does not associate with other sectarians, wanderers, mendicants, or ascetics, nor with those who follow treatises on aesthetics, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them. He does not follow or associate with those who hold the mantras of the materialists <note>original: "lokāyata" — a school of Indian materialism/skepticism</note>, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. He does not associate with outcasts, nor with boxers, nor with pork-butchers, nor with fowlers, nor with deer-hunters, <margin>N 181</margin> nor with meat-sellers, nor with actors or dancers, nor with athletes or wrestlers. He does not visit the places where others engage in sensual entertainment or play, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. If he happens to visit them, he preaches the Dharma to them from time to time, but he does so without relying on them.

He does not associate with followers of the vehicle of the disciples <note>original: "śrāvakayānīya" — followers of the lesser vehicle</note>, monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, nor does he serve, frequent, or wait upon them, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with them. He does not share the same sphere of activity with them, whether in walking or in dwelling. If he happens to visit them, he preaches the Dharma to them from time to time, but he does so without relying on them. This, Mañjuśrī, is the sphere of association of the bodhisattva and mahāsattva."

<margin>K 277</margin>
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva and mahāsattva does not preach the Dharma to women by grasping at any sign of attachment, nor does he have a desire to see women frequently. He does not visit households, nor does he think that a young girl, a maiden, or a daughter-in-law should be spoken to frequently, and he does not engage in polite conversation with them. He does not preach the Dharma to a eunuch, nor does he engage in familiar conversation with him, nor does he engage in polite conversation with him. He does not enter a house alone for the sake of begging, unless he is dwelling in the mindfulness of the Tathāgata <note>original: "tathāgatānusmṛti"</note>. If, however, he preaches the Dharma to women, he does not do so even with attachment to the Dharma."

<summary>This passage defines the "happy conduct" of a bodhisattva in the final age, emphasizing the necessity of moral discipline, avoiding worldly associations, and maintaining detachment in social interactions.</summary>
<keywords>Mañjuśrī, bodhisattva, conduct, mindfulness of the Buddha, social boundaries, Dharma</keywords>

Seeing that rain being made fruitless, the <term>Śatakratu</term> <gloss>the hundred-sacrificed one (Indra)</gloss>, the <term>Pākaśāsana</term> <gloss>the subduer of the demon Pāka (Indra)</gloss>, increased that rain even more.

<margin>Paya</margin> Then, raising a great peak of Mount <term>Mandara</term> <gloss>a mythical mountain</gloss> in his hands, complete with trees, he cast it down, desiring to kill the son of <term>Pāṇḍu</term> <gloss>Arjuna</gloss>.
Then, with arrows that were swift and had flaming tips, Arjuna shattered the mountain peak into a thousand pieces.

|| <term>Vaiśampāyana</term> <gloss>a sage and narrator</gloss> said || Terrified by the fall of that mountain, the inhabitants of <term>Khāṇḍava</term>—the <term>Dānavas</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>, <term>Rākṣasas</term> <gloss>man-eating demons</gloss>, <term>Nāgas</term> <gloss>serpent beings</gloss>, and the tree-dwelling creatures—<margin>829</margin>
Elephants in rut, tigers, and maned lions, all distraught, abandoned their own kind, and all species of beings.
They gazed upon that forest, angry and with weapons raised, and it stood as if agitated by the sound of the collapse.
Seeing the forest burning in many places, and <term>Kṛṣṇa</term> with his weapon raised, they let out a fierce cry.
By that fierce cry and by the roar of the Fire-god <note>original: "vibhāvasoḥ" (of the Fire god)</note>, the whole sky rumbled as if with storm clouds.
Then, for the destruction of them, the long-armed <term>Keśava</term> <gloss>Kṛṣṇa</gloss> released his extremely fierce, bright as the light of the sun and radiant discus <term>cakra</term>. <margin>830</margin>

Wondrous, wondrous was the discus of Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of foes; having severed many creatures, it returns to his hand again and again.
As he slaughtered the <term>Piśācas</term>, serpents, and <term>Rākṣasas</term> in this way, the appearance of the one who is the soul of all beings became most fierce. <margin>831</margin>
Among all the gathered gods, there was no one who could conquer Kṛṣṇa and the son of <term>Pāṇḍu</term> in battle.

These two, who are difficult to assail and unconquerable in battle, cannot be defeated—even among all the worlds, they are the most excellent of ancient sages.

Therefore, O <term>Vāsava</term> <gloss>Indra</gloss>, you should depart from here along with the gods. Observe that the destruction of <term>Khāṇḍava</term> is destined. <margin>833</margin>

May the love-play of Hari, as sung by Sri Jayadeva, bring an end to the impurities of the Kali Age. <note>8</note>

This moon, whose glow resembles the pale lotus-face of Murari <note>Krishna</note> during separation, though it attempts to conceal my pain, acts as a friend to Desire <note>Manobhava/Kama</note> and deeply intensifies the pangs of love within my heart. <note>5</note>

<note>The commentator notes: In this situation, the heroine is firm and steady. Regarding the verse beginning "Sri...", this love-play—or rather, the unconventional sporting—described by Sri Jayadeva should bring about the pacification of the sins of the Kali Age. As stated in the Sangeetarāja: "Where Sri-raga is the mode, the rhythm is fast, the description is of Vasudeva, and the acts are of intimacy, this is known as a superior composition." Thus, this is the fourteenth composition, known as Harimita-Champaka-Shekhara. Now, Radha, tormented by separation, addresses the moon: Aye is a gentle address. O friend, this moon actually intensifies the agony of desire in my heart. How so? It is a friend to Manobhava (Kama). It reminds me of the state of Murari's separation. How is the moon described? It possesses a luster like that of Murari's face, which has turned pale due to separation. Therefore, even though it hides the pain, it remains a friend to desire and thus causes pain. The meaning is: while the beauty of the moon, resembling Krishna's face in separation, should soothe my pain, its nature as a friend to Kama ensures it only increases my suffering. The Amarakosha states: 'lava, lesha, and kana are synonyms for a small bit'.</note>

<note>Regarding the verse "Sri Jayadeva...", the play of the enemy of Mura </note><note>Krishna</note> as sung by Jayadeva should destroy the impurities of the Kali Age for both the listeners and the reciters. Now, the poet explains how the moon causes even greater distress. "O" is an expression of sorrow. This moon, which I see, expands the agony of love in my heart to an extreme degree. How is it described? It possesses the luster of Krishna's face-lotus, which has turned pale due to my separation from him. The implication is that seeing the moon, which resembles Krishna's face, causes intense pain through the memory of that face. What is it doing? It covers or obscures the pain. The arrival of the moon uproots one's discretion, causing the mind to remember Krishna, even though he has committed an offense. The reason for its deceitfulness is given: it is a friend to Kama. Since I did not follow Krishna even when he was near, and thus violated the command of Love, Kama has become my enemy. The moon, wishing to assist Kama, also generates this distress. The moon and Kama are well-known to be friends, as both are born of the mind <note>The text cites the Vedic source: "The moon was born of the mind."</note>. The Vishva lexicon says: 'Vedana means both knowledge and pain; Aye is used in fear, anger, despair, confusion, and recollection'. The root 'tiras' means disappearance or crookedly.

If war has indeed arrived, O King, why did you not prepare for it earlier? For, who is that servant or minister who, without careful consideration, advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own post at the very start? Furthermore, one should always endeavor to conquer enemies through means other than war, as the outcome of a struggle between two combatants is never certain. Moreover, one should attempt to subdue the enemy by using diplomacy, bribery, sowing dissension, or all three combined, but never by war alone. Additionally, everyone considers themselves brave when they have not yet encountered the conflict, for who would not be proud when they have not yet seen the power of the enemy? Furthermore, one does not stir up such terrible strife among creatures, as success is rarely achieved through minor means and this new fruit is great. Therefore, seeing that war has arrived, let it be disregarded. For:

The <term>Chakravaka</term> <gloss>the ruddy sheldrake, acting as a counselor in this fable</gloss> says, "O King, war is not to be pursued. For what kind of servant or minister is it who advises a king to prepare for battle and abandon his own station without first deliberating? Furthermore, one should endeavor to conquer an opponent by means of conciliation and other strategies, but never by armed conflict, since it is impossible to know for certain which of the two combatants will emerge victorious. Moreover, one should attempt to resolve matters with an enemy by using conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension, either individually or together, but never by fighting. Besides, every person is a hero as long as they have not yet faced a battle, for who would not be arrogant without having seen the strength of another?"

One may definitely have the heart of a beast, yet because of one's appearance, one is treated with the closeness reserved for one's own kind. The traditions state that those with horns, teeth, claws, who fly, walk, crouch, or run are called birds and beasts. They do not necessarily lack the heart of a human, yet because of their appearance, they are treated with alienation. Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, and the sovereigns of the Xia dynasty had bodies like snakes, human faces, ox heads, and tiger noses. They possessed forms that were not human, yet they held the virtues of the great sages. Jie of Xia, Zhou of Shang, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu all possessed the features and seven orifices exactly the same as any human, yet they harbored the hearts of beasts. For the common people to rely solely on outward appearance to seek supreme wisdom is to remain far from the truth. The Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor on the plains of Banquan. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>a legendary ancient musical composition</gloss> was played in nine movements, the phoenix came to perform its rites.

By this time, Daiyu was already more than half recovered. Seeing Xiangling had also moved into the Garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling laughed and said, "Now that I have finally moved in and have some free time, it would be my great fortune if you would teach me how to write poetry." Daiyu laughed and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly teach you the basics." Xiangling laughed and said, "If that is really so, I will take you as my teacher. You must not get tired of it." Daiyu said, "What is difficult about it? It is nothing more than the <term>qichengzhuanhe</term> <gloss>the four-part structure of a poem: opening, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. In the middle, the development and transition are two pairs of couplets: flat tones must be paired with oblique tones; abstract concepts must be paired with concrete ones, and concrete ones with abstract. If you truly have an extraordinary line, it is acceptable even if the flat/oblique tones and the abstract/concrete pairs do not match."

Xiangling laughed and said, "No wonder when I often take an old poetry book and secretly read a few poems, there are some that are perfectly matched and others that are not. I have also heard it said that, 'the first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, while the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this, and some have errors in the second, fourth, and sixth characters. That is why I have been puzzled every day. Now that I hear you speak, it turns out that these rules are actually of little consequence; it is only important that the words and phrases are fresh and novel." Daiyu said, "That is precisely the point. The words and phrases are ultimately secondary matters; the most important thing is establishing the intent. If the sentiment and interest are genuine, even if the words and phrases are not polished, it is naturally good. This is what is called 'not letting the words harm the intent'."

Xiangling said, "I only love Lu Fangweng's <note>Lu You, a famous Song dynasty poet</note> lines, 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, the scent remains for long; the ancient inkstone is slightly worn, the gathered ink is thick,' they are truly vivid and interesting!" You should first ponder his one hundred five-character regulated verses carefully until you know them thoroughly. Then, read one hundred twenty of Old Du's <note>Du Fu, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character regulated verses. Next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>Li Bai, the Tang dynasty poet</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three people as a foundation in your belly, then take a look at Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, and Bao. Since you are such an extremely clever and sharp person, you won't need a year of effort before you become a true poetess!" Xiangling heard this and laughed, "If that is the case, good Miss, take the book out for me, and I will take it back. It will be good to recite a few poems at night." When Daiyu heard this, she ordered Zijuan to bring Wang Youcheng's <note>Another name for Wang Wei</note> five-character regulated verses and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones with red circles; they are all selected by me. Read one poem after another. If there is something you don't understand, ask your mistress; or if you meet me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Hengwu Courtyard. Ignoring all other matters, she sat under the lamp and read them one by one. Although Baochai urged her several times to sleep, she would not. Seeing her such painstaking effort, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, after Daiyu had just finished washing and combing, she saw Xiangling smilingly delivered the book, wanting to trade it for Du's regulated verses. Daiyu laughed and asked, "How many have you memorized in total?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have read all the ones marked with red circles." Daiyu said, "Have you grasped some of them?" Xiangling laughed and said, "I have grasped some, but I don't know if I'm right. Let me tell you [my thoughts] and see."

<meta>continues from previous page: Li Ru advised Dong Zhuo to appoint famous scholars to win popular support. Following this, he recommended Cai Yong for his talent, and Dong Zhuo ordered that he be summoned.</meta>

Cai Yong did not comply at first. Dong Zhuo was furious and sent a messenger to tell him, "If you do not come, I will wipe out your clan." Terrified, Cai Yong had no choice but to obey the order and arrive. Dong Zhuo was overjoyed to see him and promoted him three times in a single month, eventually appointing him as a Palace Attendant <note>original: 侍中</note>, treating him with great intimacy and favor. <gloss>He always relied on the patronage of Wang Feng and Yang Xiong; he would end his life as firewood and be buried by the woodcutters of Kunshan.</gloss>

Meanwhile, the Young Emperor <note>original: 少帝</note>, Empress Dowager He, and Consort Tang were trapped in the Yong'an Palace, with clothing and food becoming increasingly scarce. The Young Emperor’s tears never dried. <gloss>As the former king once said, the sun and moon in this place feel endless.</gloss> One day, he happened to see a pair of swallows flying in the courtyard and composed a poem. <gloss>In the empty courtyard, birds dance and fly; in this cold palace and abandoned temple, I am alone, and my years are my own.</gloss>

The poem read:

The tender grass is green, congealed in mist,
The pair of swallows flutter and fly.
The Luo River is a blue stream,
Envied by those upon the road.
<gloss>The first half of the poem describes the swallows and looks into the distance.</gloss>
Deep within the azure clouds lies my former palace,
<gloss>Gazing at the old palace, unable to fly, truly not as fortunate as the pair of swallows returning to their old nest. How tragic.</gloss>
Who will wield loyalty and righteousness,
To vent the grievances in my heart?
<gloss>The second half is an expression of his personal wishes. A fine poem.</gloss>

Dong Zhuo often sent people to eavesdrop. That day, they intercepted this poem and presented it to him. Dong Zhuo said, "He is full of resentment and writes poems. I have a valid reason to kill him." <gloss>Killing him provides a famous justification, setting an example for the world.</gloss>

He then ordered Li Ru to take eighteen armed men into the palace to murder the Emperor. The Emperor and his consorts were on the upper floor when a palace maid reported that Li Ru had arrived. The Emperor was terrified. Li Ru presented the Emperor with a cup of poisoned wine. <gloss>Suggesting that such a poem deserves this wine, which is the most elegant way to end him.</gloss>

text:
荀子 正論

In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had a thousand officials, and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. Because of these thousand officials, orders were carried out throughout the states of the Middle Kingdom; such a ruler was called a King. Because of these hundred officials, orders were carried out within their own borders; even if a state was not secure, it did not reach the point of collapse, being replaced, or perishing <note>original note: 遂 (sui) is read as 墜 (zhui), meaning to let one's enterprise fall.</note>, and such a ruler was called a Lord. This is the case after the descendants of the Sage Kings have possessed the world and hold the registers of the state, serving as the ancestral house of the world. However, if they are untalented and not centered <note>original note: 不中 (bu zhong) means not centered or upright.</note>, then internally the hundred surnames will suffer, and externally the feudal lords will rebel. Those near them within their borders will not be unified, and those far away, the feudal lords, will not listen. Their orders will not be carried out within their own borders; in extreme cases, the feudal lords will encroach upon them, diminish their territory, and attack them. If things reach this state, even if they have not yet perished, I say they have lost the world. 

When the Sage Kings have passed away and those who hold the registers are weak and unable to secure <note>original note: 罷 (pi) is read as weak and unable to handle affairs; 縣 (xuan) means to secure or fasten.</note> the world, the world has no lord. If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is clear and whose prestige has accumulated, the people within the seas will all wish for him to be their lord and teacher. If there is a tyrannical state that is uniquely extravagant and unrestrained, how then can one punish it <note>original note: 暴國 (bao guo) refers to states like those of Jie and Zhou; 獨侈 (du chi) refers to being unrestrained; 安 (an) is similar to "then".</note>? One must not harm the innocent people, but punish the ruler of the tyrannical state as if punishing a solitary fellow <note>original note: 獨夫 (du fu) refers to a person whom the whole world refuses to help, as if he were a man standing alone.</note>. If one can do this, it can be said that one is able to use the world. Being able to use the world is what is called being a King. 

Tang and Wu did not seize the world; they cultivated their Way, practiced their righteousness, shared the common benefits of the world, and eliminated the common harms of the world, and so the world returned to them <note>original note: This implies the world gave its allegiance of its own accord.</note>. Jie and Zhou did not cast away the world; they turned against the virtues of Yu and Tang, threw the distinctions of ritual and righteousness into chaos, behaved like beasts, accumulated their evils, and exhausted those beneath them.

<summary>This passage defines the distinction between a true King and a mere Lord, arguing that legitimacy is based on virtue and the welfare of the people rather than inherited position alone. It concludes by contrasting the righteous success of Tang and Wu with the self-destructive tyranny of Jie and Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Xunzi, Correct Argument, Kingly Way, Tang and Wu, Jie and Zhou, Ritual and Righteousness</keywords>

# Brahma Sutra Bhashya | [Adhyaya 3, Pada 3, Adhikarana 7, Sutra 14]

It is the Supreme Being alone that is presented as superior to all of these; therefore, it is appropriate that each one is not declared superior. Why? Because there is no purpose. For no purpose is seen or heard in the superiority of the others being established. However, when the Person <term>purusha</term> <gloss>the Conscious Subject</gloss> is understood as being beyond the senses and the rest, and beyond all objective phenomena, a purpose is seen: the attainment of liberation <term>moksha</term> <gloss>release</gloss>. And so the scripture says: "By discerning this, one is released from the mouth of death" (Katha Upanishad 3.15). Moreover, by showing reverence for the subject of the Person through the denial of anything else and the use of the word 'limit' <term>kastha</term> <gloss>the final point or limit</gloss>, the text shows that the sequence from the former to the latter is for the realization of the Person. The phrase "for the sake of the narrative" means for the sake of the correct knowledge preceded by a narrative. This narrative is indeed taught only for the sake of correct knowledge, not because the narrative itself is the primary focus. 14

**And because of the word 'Self'. 15**

For this reason also, the description of the sequence of the senses and the rest is meant for the realization of the Person. The reason is that the text refers to the Person under discussion as the Self: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth. But it is seen by the subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect" (Katha Upanishad 3.12). Hence, it is understood that the non-selfhood of the others is intended. It also shows that the Person is difficult to know and requires a refined mind to be understood. For the sake of that knowledge, the text prescribes the narrative: "The wise man should restrain his speech into the mind" (Katha Upanishad 3.13). That has been explained in the section "Even that which is inferred is mentioned by some" (Brahma Sutra 1.4.1). In this way, by manifold methods—

**Bhamati**

The Veda, by the sign of the negation of others and the sign of being the substrate of all things, shows the purport lies in the Person. Thus, he says 'Moreover' <term>apica</term>, to show that the statement of superiority of each previous one over the subsequent one is intended for that purpose. He connects the sutra 'for the sake of the narrative' by explaining that the superiority of one over the other is for the sake of seeing the Person, as there is no independent purpose in the others. 14 'And because of the word Self'. Furthermore, because of the consistency between the opening and closing statements—"That is the highest abode of Vishnu" and "There is nothing superior to the Person"—it is certain that the whole passage aims at a single Person. Thus, it is not appropriate to assume a difference in sentences or a difference in results, as it would be cumbersome. 15

**Nyaya Nirnaya**

'Why?' He considers that the purport is not meant for the others because they lack the capacity to produce the desired result. 'No purpose'—he asks how the absence of purpose is stated, and he differentiates between fruit established by logical analysis and fruit established by scripture. He says 'No' to the first. He replies to the second, 'is heard'. Since this passage is seen to concern the nature of reality, it is not suited for the injunction of meditation; it concerns the knowledge of the ultimate goal of human life. Since the inner self is the goal, the senses do not have independent status as the goal, so the knowledge of each one's superiority is not the aim. If the knowledge of the Person's superiority were also fruitlessly, how could there be a causal relationship to the human goal? He says 'However, in the Person' because, as the subject of the ultimate, the knowledge of the Person is not empty and is experiential. 'Is seen'—he maintains that since the cessation of ignorance and false knowledge is a visible fruit, it is not right to imagine an unseen one. Regarding the experience of the wise, he cites the scripture 'And so'. He says 'Moreover' because the entire context aims at the knowledge of the Person. 'Superior to the Person'—the Veda shows reverence for the Person by the sign of negation and the word 'limit' as a boundary. The sequence of former to latter is the statement of the superiority of the latter over the former. Since there is no injunction for meditation here, how can the knowledge of the Person be for meditation? He explains the part of the sutra: 'for the sake of the narrative'. The knowledge of the attributeless Brahman is also for the sake of meditation as it resides in Brahman, but he clarifies that it is consistent with the scripture 'Then he who...'. 14 He gives another reason for the Person being the only subject here: 'And because of the word Self'. He explains the word 'and' in the sutra: 'For this reason also'. Explaining clearly, he breaks down the word 'Self'. He refutes the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural: 'But it is seen'. He says 'under discussion' because of the Selfhood in that scripture. He states the intended meaning of the sutra: 'Hence'. He explains the rest of the earlier meaning: 'of that'. He states the purport of the later part: 'refined mind'. He gives the other reason indicated by the word 'and': 'That'. Regarding the doubt that only the restraint of speech is mentioned in the mantra, not an injunction for meditation, he says 'That has been explained'. The meaning is that since the Self is difficult to know by scripture itself, and the senses are easy to know, the declaration of their superiority is a device for the purport. Srimad Bhagavad Gita

[Chapter 9, Verses 30-31]

Shridhara Swami’s Commentary: If You grant liberation only to Your devotees, and not to non-devotees, does this mean You possess partiality born of attachment or aversion? Addressing this, He says, "I am the same." I am equal toward all beings; therefore, there is no one who is dear to Me or detestable to Me. Although this is true, those who worship Me, they are in Me as devotees, and I am in them as the Bestower of Grace. The essence is this: just as fire does not act with partiality when it removes the suffering of cold and darkness only for those who approach it, or just as the wish-fulfilling tree <note>The <term>kalpavriksha</term> <gloss>wish-fulfilling tree of Hindu mythology</gloss></note> acts without bias, similarly, there is no partiality in Me, even though I favor My devotees. Rather, this is the inherent greatness of devotion to Me. (29)

Madhusudana Saraswati’s Commentary: Furthermore, the greatness of devotion to Me is such that it creates this appearance of partiality even in One who is equal. Hear of that greatness:

> Even if a person of very wicked conduct worships Me with single-minded devotion, he is to be regarded as righteous, for he has resolved correctly. (30)

Whoever he may be, even if he is a person of very wicked conduct, like Ajamila, if he worships Me with single-minded devotion—serving Me due to the dawning of some past merit—he, though previously unrighteous, must be regarded as righteous. For he has resolved correctly; that is, he has attained a righteous determination. (30)

Shridhara Swami’s Commentary: Furthermore, showing that the power of devotion to Me is beyond logic, He says, "Even if." Even a man of extremely wicked conduct, if he worships only Me—Shri Narayana—without practicing devotion to other deities, he is to be regarded as righteous, as excellent. Because he has resolved correctly; he has made the firm determination that "I shall be fulfilled by worshipping the Supreme Lord alone." (30)

Madhusudana Saraswati’s Commentary: Because of this very correct determination, he abandons his wicked conduct:

> Quickly he becomes a soul of righteousness and attains lasting peace. O son of Kunti, proclaim that My devotee never perishes. (31)

Even one who was unrighteous for a long time quickly becomes a soul of righteousness—one whose mind follows righteousness—due to the greatness of worshipping Me. He abandons his wicked conduct instantly and becomes well-behaved. Moreover, he attains lasting peace; he thoroughly attains permanent cessation of the desire for sense objects, due to extreme detachment. One might think: "Perhaps a devotee of Mine, not having abandoned his previously practiced wicked conduct, might not become righteous, and thus he would surely perish." Denying this, out of compassion for His devotees, the Lord speaks as if provoked: Do not consider this a wonder, O son of Kunti. The greatness of devotion to Me is certainly such as this. Therefore, even in front of those who are skeptical, make a promise. Make this pledge with boldness and confidence: "My devotee—the devotee of Vasudeva—even if he is of very wicked conduct, even if he faces a crisis of life, even if he is entreated by those worthy of things hard to attain, even if he is extremely ignorant or without shelter, does not perish. Rather, he is fulfilled."

(2) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** When there is an extremely intense craving for eating meat, one should counteract that desire in this manner. It does not mean that killing animals is permitted. Regarding the phrase "he should make," it refers to a "ghee-animal" <note>a figure or representation of an animal made of clarified butter</note>, which is a modification of ghee, and because it has the same form as animal flesh, it is called an animal. Similarly, there is a "flour-animal." Regarding "attachment" <term>saṅge</term> <gloss>intense desire</gloss>, some say it refers to overcoming the elemental nature, but since that is not the common worldly understanding, this implies only that [the alternative is necessary]. 37

(3) **Kullūka:** "Attachment" refers to being addicted to eating meat. One should make an imitation animal out of ghee or flour and eat that. One should never desire to kill animals without the specific purpose of a sacrifice to the deities. 37

(4) **Rāghavānanda:** "Ghee-animal" means an animal imitation made of ghee. "Attachment" refers to the inclination toward animal sacrifice, or being addicted to eating meat, or [this rule applies to] essential customary duties, but not to Vedic rituals, because that would contradict the [prescribed] eleven sacrificial animals. Therefore, it is said that slaughter in a sacrifice is not [considered] slaughter. 37

(5) **Nandana:** [The author] states one should not perform violence according to the [standard] method, but says "he should make" [an alternative]. "In attachment" means on occasions of festivals and similar events where relatives and others are gathered; one should prepare a "ghee-animal." In place of an animal, one should offer an abundance of ghee or flour cakes. 37

(6) **Rāmacandra:** One should make a "ghee-animal" when there is attachment [to eating meat]. One should do the same with a "flour-animal." One should never desire to kill an animal in vain. 37

### As many hairs as the animal has, so many times in every future birth will the slayer of an animal in vain undergo slaughter. 38

(1) **Medhātithi:** He suffers slaughter as many times [as there are hairs] in his births. A "slayer of an animal in vain" is one who kills an animal without the injunctions of the Vedas or Smṛtis. This is often done by hunters and others for worldly pursuits. The word <term>paśughnaḥ</term> <gloss>animal-slayer</gloss> is a Vedic grammatical form. 38

(2) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" means that many number of occasions. "Slayer of an animal in vain" refers to one who kills an animal not prescribed by the Vedas or Smṛtis. 38

(3) **Kullūka:** He who kills animals for his own sake without intending them for the deities is a "slayer of an animal in vain." When he dies, he will undergo slaughter in birth after birth, for as many times as there are hairs on the animal's body. Therefore, one should not kill an animal in vain. The suffix <term>kṛtvasuc</term> is used here to denote the repetition of an action. The particle <term>ha</term> here is used to indicate a well-known scriptural tradition. 38

(4) **Rāghavānanda:** [The author] states the punishment for the opposite [behavior] with "as many as." Here, the particle <term>ha</term> denotes something well-established. 38

(5) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that many number of instances. The particle <term>ha</term> is used to express compassion. 38

(6) **Rāmacandra:** A man who is a "slayer of an animal in vain," having committed slaughter in this world against the laws of righteousness, attains animal-hood birth after birth, proportional to the number of hairs—eight crores <note>80 million</note> of hairs. 38

### Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice, for the prosperity of this whole universe. Therefore, slaughter in a sacrifice is not [considered] slaughter. 39

(1) **Medhātithi:** This does not contradict the fault mentioned previously. Regarding the slaughter enjoined by the Vedas and Smṛtis that constitutes a component of the sacrifice, it is intended precisely for the sake of that prosperity. "Created" means produced by Prajāpati, the Lord of Creatures. "By himself" is an <term>arthavāda</term> <gloss>praise/explanatory statement</gloss>. The "sacrifice" for this world refers to rites like the <term>Jyotiṣṭoma</term>. "Prosperity" means growth, nourishment, and expansion. Therefore, that slaughter is to be known as "not slaughter." This is stated because of the removal of the sin that arises from violence. 39

(2) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** Here, he removes the doubt regarding why there is no such fault when killing for the sake of sacrifice by saying "for the sake of sacrifice." It is for the prosperity of the world, for birth, and for the generation of living beings through the continuous cycle of sacrificial offerings, the nourishment of the sun, rain, and seeds. By this, it is stated that because a single animal sacrifice leads to the welfare of many beings, such a fault does not exist. 39

<summary>This page discusses the ethical handling of meat consumption and animal sacrifice, distinguishing between ritual killing and vain slaughter, while arguing that Vedic sacrifices contribute to the cosmic order.</summary>

[Section 4: On Deposits] Mitakshara Commentary

The deposit, if lost or stolen due to fate, water, fire, or thieves, is not to be repaid by the one with whom it was deposited. The loss of that wealth belongs to the owner, provided it was not brought about by dishonest means. As **Narada** says: "If a deposit is lost along with the property of the one who accepted it, the loss is that of the owner. This holds true for losses caused by fate or the king, provided it was not brought about by dishonest conduct."

An exception to this is stated:

### If a loss occurs when it is sought and not returned, he must pay its value and an equal fine. || 66 ||

If the owner requests or demands the return of the deposit and the holder does not return it, then even if the loss occurs later due to the king or other causes, the holder must pay the value of that property to the owner and pay an equal amount as a fine to the king. || 66 ||

Regarding the fine for one who makes use of the deposit:

### He who uses it by his own will is to be fined and must return it with interest.

He who, without the owner's permission, makes use of the deposited property or engages in trade with it for profit, is to be fined according to the scale of enjoyment or the profit gained. He must also restore the deposit to the owner, with interest if it was used for personal enjoyment, or with the accrued profit if it was used in trade. The rate of interest is stated by **Katyayana**: "If a deposit, the surplus of interest, a purchase, or a sale is not returned when demanded, it increases at five percent per hundred." This is applicable when the deposit has been consumed. However, for property lost due to negligence or ignorance, a specific rule is shown by the same author: "One must pay the consumed deposit with interest; a deposit lost due to neglect must be paid back in equal amount; and one that is lost through ignorance should be repaid slightly less." "Slightly less" means reduced by one-fourth.

The rules for deposits are extended to requested items and others:

### This rule applies to requested items, secondary deposits, trusts, and special deposits. || 67 ||

**Requested** (<term>Yachita</term> <gloss>an item borrowed for a specific occasion, such as clothing or ornaments for a wedding</gloss>) refers to items brought after being requested. A **secondary deposit** (<term>Anvahita</term> <gloss>an item deposited by a custodian into the hands of another with the instruction to hand it over to the original owner</gloss>) is when an item deposited in one person's hands is later deposited by that person into the hands of another with the instruction that it be given to the owner. A **trust** (<term>Nyasa</term> <gloss>property left in a house without informing the head of the house, to be returned to the owner</gloss>) is when an item is placed in the care of household members without the knowledge of the head of the house, intended for delivery to the owner. A **special deposit** (<term>Nikshepa</term> <gloss>property handed over in the presence of the depositary</gloss>) is one made in the owner's presence. The term "and others" includes gold or other materials left with a goldsmith for the making of bracelets and the like, as well as **reciprocal deposits** (<term>pratinyasa</term> <gloss>an arrangement where both parties agree to look after each other's goods</gloss>), where one says to the other, "I will protect this of yours, and you protect this of mine." As **Narada** says: "This very rule is observed for requested items, secondary deposits, and so on; for items left with craftsmen, for standard deposits, for trusts, and for reciprocal deposits." In all these cases—requested items, secondary deposits, and so on—this rule, which is the same as the rule for the return of a standard deposit, should be understood. || 67 ||

->End of the Section on Deposits.<-

<summary>This page defines the legal responsibilities of a custodian regarding deposits, specifying that the custodian is not liable for losses caused by fate, unless negligence or dishonest conduct is involved. It further outlines fines for the unauthorized use of deposits and extends these legal frameworks to borrowed items, trusts, and other custodial arrangements.</summary>
<keywords>Deposit, Liability, Fine, Narada, Katyayana, Custodian, Property Law, Mitakshara</keywords>

VALĀHAKAVAGGA. 103

1. These four, monks, are clouds. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain. 
These, monks, are the four types of clouds.

2. Just so, monks, these four individuals like unto clouds are found in the world. Which four? 
Those that thunder but do not rain... (and so on)... and those that both thunder and rain.

3. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that thunders but does not rain? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term> <gloss>teaching</gloss>: discourses, songs, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, sayings, birth stories, marvelous events, and analytical descriptions. Yet, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who thunders but does not rain. Just as that cloud, monks, thunders but does not rain, so do I compare this individual to it.

4. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that rains but does not thunder? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... (and so on)... analytical descriptions. Yet, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... (and so on)... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who rains but does not thunder. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

5. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that neither thunders nor rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual does not learn the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... he does not understand as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who neither thunders nor rains. Just as that cloud, monks... I compare him to it.

6. And how, monks, is an individual like a cloud that both thunders and rains? 
Here, monks, a certain individual learns the <term>Dhamma</term>: discourses... analytical descriptions. Furthermore, he understands as it really is: "This is suffering"... he understands as it really is: "This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering." In this way, monks, an individual is one who both thunders and rains. Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains, so do I compare this individual to it.

<summary>This page presents an analogy between four types of rain clouds and four types of people based on their knowledge of Buddhist doctrine and their realization of the Four Noble Truths.</summary>

The supreme <term>Maheśvara</term> <gloss>the Great Lord</gloss> is omniscient, the creator of the mother of the entire universe. How is He to be known? Through inference or through effort? For example, the inference is as follows: the object under dispute, which is perceived, must have a cause, because it comes into existence and will cease to exist, like a painting. From this, what is understood in general is known in particular through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>meditation/disciplined union</gloss>. For the individual soul, realization comes from one's own experience. The activity of <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primordial nature</gloss> is for the purpose of discriminating between these two, the supreme and the individual. Its purpose for another will be explained later. And its purpose for itself: it remains indifferent toward that <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>conscious spirit</gloss> to whom it has already revealed itself through discrimination. How can <term>prakṛti</term>, which is unconscious, be active? It is observed that even unconscious things, such as milk, act for a purpose, such as the result of fruit etc.

Now, regarding who is eligible for liberation, the text says:

**Through detachment, that is accomplished.**

And so the scripture says: "Rising above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worldly status, they then wander, living on alms." Also: "Having become peaceful, self-controlled, retired from sensory objects, patient, and collected, one sees the Self within the Self."

If liberation followed immediately after hearing the teachings due to detachment, then everyone would attain liberation after the guru's instruction, but this is not observed. Regarding this, the text says:

**Not by hearing alone is that accomplished, due to the strength of beginningless tendencies.**

Liberation does not occur immediately after hearing; rather, due to the strength of beginningless tendencies, for some liberation is swift, while for others it is delayed.

The text offers another reason:

○ 3. Explanation.
Regarding these six types of defilement, they are matched in reverse order to the six coarse marks. The first four and the latter three subtle marks are, according to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, Volume One, identical to this. This first section matches the three and four within the coarse marks, totaling six; thus, these names are borrowed to categorize these six.

It is also the meaning of the increase of views and desires of the aforementioned consciousness; it is also the aspect of "discriminated attachment" among the four marks mentioned above. Since the coarse mind externally attaches and corresponds to objects, polluting pure practice, it is called "defiled." "Faith-correspondence" refers to the ten stages of understanding and beyond, where the root of faith is perfected and never lost; thus, it is called faith-correspondence. ### The Seventh Section: On Neither Attainment Nor Discourse

Subhuti, what do you think? Has the Tathagata attained the <term>anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening</gloss>? Does the Tathagata have any dharma to speak of?

Subhuti replied: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma called the unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening, and there is also no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak of. Why? Because the dharma spoken by the Tathagata cannot be grasped, cannot be spoken of, and is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Why is this? Because all sages and saints are distinguished by the <term>asamskrta-dharma</term> <gloss>unconditioned dharma; that which is not created or subject to change</gloss>.

### The Eighth Section: The Birth of Merit through the Dharma

Subhuti, what do you think? If a person were to fill the three-thousand great thousand-fold world system with the seven treasures and use them for charity, would the merit gained by this person be great?

Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One. Why? Because this merit is not of the nature of true merit, and therefore the Tathagata speaks of the merit as great.

If, however, there were another person who, within this sutra, received and upheld even a four-line stanza and explained it to others, their merit would exceed the former. Why? Subhuti, all Buddhas and the dharma of the unsurpassed, complete, perfect awakening of all Buddhas arise from this sutra. Subhuti, what is called the Buddhadharma is precisely not the Buddhadharma.

<note>The following section explains the structure of the reply, consisting of three parts: stating the number of reasons, explaining their characteristics, and providing a summary.</note>

The reply states: There are eight types of reasons and conditions. What are these eight?
<note>In explaining the characteristics, the first is the general reason, and the subsequent seven are specific. The reason for this arrangement is that the general category covers the fundamental intent, while the specific categories address the particular needs of the recipients.</note>

1. The first is the general characteristic of the reasons and conditions. This refers to the intention to enable all sentient beings to depart from all suffering and attain ultimate happiness. Regarding the departure from all suffering within this general intent, it means enabling sentient beings to move away from the three sufferings <note>suffering of suffering, suffering of change, and suffering of conditioning</note> and the two types of death <note>the death of changing manifestations and the death of delusion</note>. Regarding the attainment of ultimate happiness, it means enabling them to attain the joy of supreme enlightenment <term>anuttara-samyak-sambodhi</term> <gloss>unsurpassed complete enlightenment</gloss> and great nirvana. This does not refer to seeking worldly fame and profit, etc. There are two interpretations of this: first, it means not seeking the benefits and pleasures of human or heavenly realms in future lives.
